concepts.def: The process by which individuals with characteristics most suited to the environment are more likely to survive to breed successfully, so that the characteristics which have enabled these individuals to survive are then passed on to the next generation. Charles Darwin proposed the theory of evolution by natural selection as a result of observations on a round the world expedition, backed by years of experimentation and discussion and linked to developing knowledge of geology and fossils.

The differences between individuals of the same species. Individual organisms within a particular species show a wide range of variation for a characteristic, and this variation is already present in the population before natural selection acts on it.
The book in which Darwin published his ideas about evolution by natural selection in 1859. There was much controversy surrounding these revolutionary new ideas.

The theory of evolution by natural selection was only gradually accepted because the theory challenged the idea that God made all the animals and plants that live on Earth, because there was insufficient evidence at the time the theory was published to convince many scientists, and because the mechanism of inheritance and variation was not known until 50 years after the theory was published.

Another theory of how species change, proposed by Jean-Baptiste Lamarck, based mainly on the idea that changes that occur in an organism during its lifetime can be inherited. We now know that in the vast majority of cases this type of inheritance cannot occur.

The scientist who independently proposed the theory of evolution by natural selection. He published joint writings with Darwin in 1858 which prompted Darwin to publish On the Origin of Species (1859) the following year. Wallace worked worldwide gathering evidence for evolutionary theory and is best known for his work on warning colouration in animals and his theory of speciation.
The formation of new species. Alfred Wallace did much pioneering work on speciation, but more evidence over time has led to our current understanding of the theory of speciation.

concepts.term: Steps that give rise to a new species
concepts.def: Populations of a species become isolated from one another and experience different conditions. There is variation within each population, and natural selection means that individuals with the characteristics most suited to their own environment are more likely to survive to breed successfully and pass those characteristics on. Over many generations the two populations become so different that they can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring, so they are two species.

In the mid-19th Century Gregor Mendel carried out breeding experiments on plants. One of his observations was that the inheritance of each characteristic is determined by 'units' that are passed on to descendants unchanged.

concepts.term: Why Mendel's discovery was not recognised in his lifetime
concepts.def: Mendel worked in the mid-19th Century, before the behaviour of chromosomes during cell division had been observed, so there was no known structure that could carry his 'units'. The significance of his discovery was therefore not appreciated by scientists at the time and was only recognised after his death.

In the late 19th Century the behaviour of chromosomes during cell division was observed. In the early 20th Century it was observed that chromosomes and Mendel's 'units' behaved in similar ways, and this led to the idea that the 'units', now called genes, were located on chromosomes.

concepts.term: Structure of DNA and gene theory
concepts.def: In the mid-20th Century the structure of DNA was determined and the mechanism of gene function was worked out. This scientific work by many scientists led to the gene theory being developed.

Evidence for Darwin's theory is now available as it has been shown that characteristics are passed on to offspring in genes. There is further evidence in the fossil record and in the knowledge of how resistance to antibiotics evolves in bacteria. Because of this evidence the theory of evolution by natural selection is now widely accepted, which is the impact these ideas have had on biology.
The 'remains' of organisms from millions of years ago, which are found in rocks.

Fossils may be formed from parts of organisms that have not decayed because one or more of the conditions needed for decay are absent, when parts of the organism are replaced by minerals as they decay, or as preserved traces of organisms, such as footprints, burrows and rootlet traces.

concepts.term: Gaps in the early fossil record
concepts.def: Many early forms of life were soft-bodied, which means that they have left few traces behind. What traces there were have been mainly destroyed by geological activity. This is why scientists cannot be certain about how life began on Earth.

A diagram, built from evidence such as the fossil record, in which a branch point shows a common ancestor shared by the organisms on the branches above it. Evolutionary trees and other charts, graphs and tables let us learn from fossils how much or how little different organisms have changed as life developed on Earth.
Extinctions occur when there are no remaining individuals of a species still alive.

A species may become extinct because of changes to the environment over geological time, new predators, new diseases, new more successful competitors, or a single catastrophic event such as a massive volcanic eruption or a collision with an asteroid.
Bacteria can evolve rapidly because they reproduce at a fast rate.

Mutations of bacterial pathogens produce new strains. Some strains might be resistant to antibiotics, and so are not killed. They survive and reproduce, so the population of the resistant strain rises. The resistant strain will then spread because people are not immune to it and there is no effective treatment.
A strain of bacteria which is resistant to antibiotics.

concepts.term: Reducing the development of resistant strains
concepts.def: To reduce the rate of development of antibiotic resistant strains, doctors should not prescribe antibiotics inappropriately, such as treating non-serious or viral infections; patients should complete their course of antibiotics so all bacteria are killed and none survive to mutate and form resistant strains; and the agricultural use of antibiotics should be restricted.
The development of new antibiotics is costly and slow. It is unlikely to keep up with the emergence of new resistant strains.

mcqs.q: In a beetle population, shell thickness varies. Predators cannot eat the thickest-shelled beetles. After many generations most beetles have thick shells. Why?
options: Beetles grew thicker shells in life and passed them on.
Thick-shelled beetles survived to breed and passed this on.
Beetles needed thicker shells, so they grew them to survive.
Predators made thick shells appear in the beetle population.
mcqs.explain: Individuals with characteristics most suited to the environment are more likely to survive to breed successfully, and the characteristics that have enabled these individuals to survive are then passed on to the next generation.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a reason why the theory of evolution by natural selection was only gradually accepted?
options: Scientists in 1859 were at once convinced by the evidence.
The mechanism of inheritance was not known for 50 more years.
Lamarck had shown that changes made in life are inherited.
Darwin had already explained inheritance in terms of genes.
mcqs.explain: The mechanism of inheritance and variation was not known until 50 years after the theory was published, which is one of the reasons given for the theory being only gradually accepted.

mcqs.q: Giraffes with longer necks can reach more leaves. How would a biologist today explain why giraffes now have long necks?
options: Reaching high leaves created the long neck characteristic.
Necks stretched during life were passed to the offspring.
Giraffes needed longer necks, so their necks became longer.
Giraffes with longer necks survived and bred more often.
mcqs.explain: Individuals with characteristics most suited to the environment are more likely to survive to breed successfully, and those characteristics are then passed on to the next generation.

mcqs.q: What was Alfred Russel Wallace's contribution to the theory of evolution by natural selection?
options: He collected specimens overseas for Darwin's new book.
He explained natural selection using genes and DNA.
He proposed the same theory independently of Darwin.
He convinced other scientists to accept the theory.
mcqs.explain: Alfred Russel Wallace independently proposed the theory of evolution by natural selection and published joint writings with Darwin in 1858, which prompted Darwin to publish On the Origin of Species the following year.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the theory of speciation is correct?
options: More evidence has changed our understanding over time.
Wallace gathered the evidence for Darwin's own ideas.
Two groups are new species once they look different.
Wallace's ideas on speciation were accepted at once.
mcqs.explain: Alfred Wallace did much pioneering work on speciation but more evidence over time has led to our current understanding of the theory of speciation.

mcqs.q: Two populations of one snail species are separated by a new river. What must finally happen for them to become two different species?
options: They must look different enough to be told apart by eye.
They must change during life and pass these changes on.
They must not be able to breed to give fertile young.
The river must create new characteristics in each group.
mcqs.explain: The isolated populations experience different conditions, so natural selection selects different characteristics in each. Over many generations they become so different that they can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring, and they are then two species.

mcqs.q: What did Mendel conclude from his breeding experiments on plants?
options: That genes made of DNA are carried on the chromosomes.
That the environment creates a plant's characteristics.
That plant breeding could not explain inheritance.
That 'units' pass on each characteristic unchanged.
mcqs.explain: One of Mendel's observations was that the inheritance of each characteristic is determined by 'units' that are passed on to descendants unchanged.

mcqs.q: Why was the importance of Mendel's discovery not recognised until after his death?
options: His breeding results were later shown to be incorrect.
He had described genes before DNA had been discovered.
His work was accepted by other scientists straight away.
The behaviour of chromosomes had not yet been seen.
mcqs.explain: Mendel worked in the mid-19th Century. Behaviour of chromosomes during cell division was only observed in the late 19th Century, and only in the early 20th Century was it observed that chromosomes and Mendel's 'units' behaved in similar ways.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the development of our understanding of genetics is correct?
options: Darwin used genes to explain variation when he published.
Chromosome behaviour was observed after Mendel's work.
Mendel discovered DNA during his experiments on plants.
Mendel's 'units' were rejected once chromosomes were seen.
mcqs.explain: Mendel carried out his breeding experiments in the mid-19th Century; in the late 19th Century behaviour of chromosomes during cell division was observed, and in the early 20th Century it was observed that chromosomes and Mendel's 'units' behaved in similar ways, leading to the idea that the 'units', now called genes, were located on chromosomes.

mcqs.q: What happened in the mid-20th Century in the development of gene theory?
options: Mendel described the first genes made of DNA in plants.
Darwin's theory explained inheritance by using genes.
Mendel's 'units' were proved wrong by chromosome work.
The structure of DNA and gene function were worked out.
mcqs.explain: In the mid-20th Century the structure of DNA was determined and the mechanism of gene function worked out. This scientific work by many scientists led to the gene theory being developed.

mcqs.q: Which observation is evidence that supports the theory of evolution by natural selection?
options: Antibiotic resistance evolves in bacterial populations.
Dead organisms are turned into fossils in the rocks.
Animals that exercise pass strength to their young.
The fossil record gives us a complete history of life.
mcqs.explain: Evidence for Darwin's theory is now available in the fossil record and in the knowledge of how resistance to antibiotics evolves in bacteria, and it has been shown that characteristics are passed on to offspring in genes. The theory is now widely accepted.

mcqs.q: Which statement about how fossils are formed is correct?
options: Bones and shells are kept, but footprints are not.
A dead organism will turn into a fossil in the rock.
Traces such as footprints and burrows are preserved.
The fossil record includes each species from the past.
mcqs.explain: Fossils may be formed as preserved traces of organisms, such as footprints, burrows and rootlet traces, as well as from undecayed parts and from parts replaced by minerals as they decay.

mcqs.q: Why can scientists not be certain about how life began on Earth?
options: Scientists have now collected the earliest fossils.
Early organisms had bones which dissolved in rocks.
Early life was soft-bodied and left few traces behind.
Early organisms became fossils that we can study.
mcqs.explain: Many early forms of life were soft-bodied, which means that they have left few traces behind, and what traces there were have been mainly destroyed by geological activity.

mcqs.q: An evolutionary tree shows species P and Q meeting at a branch point, with species R branching off much earlier. What does the tree show?
options: P and Q share a more recent common ancestor than R.
Species Q evolved directly from species P over time.
P and Q are separate species as they look different.
The tree shows each of the species that has lived.
mcqs.explain: A branch point on an evolutionary tree represents an ancestor shared by the organisms above it, so the later the branch point, the more recently the organisms shared an ancestor and the less they have changed from each other.

mcqs.q: A species of bird disappears from Earth after a volcanic eruption destroys its habitat. Which statement is correct?
options: The species is extinct once its numbers fall very low.
Human hunting is what makes a species become extinct.
Fossils show the exact date each species died out.
A catastrophic event can cause a species to die out.
mcqs.explain: Extinctions occur when there are no remaining individuals of a species still alive, and a single catastrophic event such as a massive volcanic eruption is one of the factors which may contribute to extinction.

mcqs.q: A patient's MRSA infection is not killed by an antibiotic. Why has the population of the resistant strain risen?
options: Resistant bacteria survived and reproduced rapidly.
The antibiotic changed the bacteria so they resist it.
The bacteria needed to resist, so they became resistant.
Each bacterium became resistant and passed this on.
mcqs.explain: Some strains produced by mutation might be resistant to antibiotics, and so are not killed. They survive and reproduce, so the population of the resistant strain rises, and bacteria can evolve rapidly because they reproduce at a fast rate.

mcqs.q: Which action would reduce the rate of development of antibiotic resistant strains?
options: Prescribing antibiotics to treat viral infections.
Restricting the use of antibiotics in agriculture.
Stopping a course of antibiotics when symptoms go.
Relying on new antibiotics being developed quickly.
mcqs.explain: The agricultural use of antibiotics should be restricted, which is one of the measures given for reducing the rate of development of antibiotic resistant strains.
